analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates up to 35% and ends tax breaks for profits moved offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced April 10, 2024 with 2 cosponsors, it died when the House Ways and Means Committee took no action beyond referral before Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise corporate income taxes substantially, restoring graduated rates that climb to 35% on large profits instead of today's flat 21%. It would also end a set of rules that let US-based multinational companies avoid or delay US tax on profits booked overseas, including loopholes for foreign subsidiaries, companies that moved their headquarters abroad on paper, and interest payments shifted to foreign affiliates. The added revenue would come almost entirely from large multinational corporations and their shareholders.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in the sense that the bill raises its revenue from corporations rather than households, and the additional corporate tax receipts could fund public services or reduce deficits. Domestic-only businesses that pay the full US rate would also compete on more equal footing with multinationals that currently shift profits offshore. Shareholders of companies with little foreign activity would see little change, while the burden falls on multinationals.

how_it_helps.text: Restores graduated corporate tax rates — 15% on the first $50,000 of income climbing to 35% on income over $10 million — replacing the flat 21% rate, effective for tax years after 2024.

Ends deferral of tax on offshore profits: all income of foreign subsidiaries controlled by US shareholders would count as immediately taxable 'subpart F' income, so US companies could no longer park profits abroad untaxed.
Requires the foreign tax credit to be calculated country by country, preventing companies from mixing taxes paid in high-tax countries with income parked in low-tax havens.
Repeals the 'check-the-box' rules and the CFC look-through rule that currently let companies make foreign subsidiary income disappear for US tax purposes.
Caps interest deductions for US members of international corporate groups, targeting the practice of loading US operations with debt to related foreign affiliates to shrink US taxable profit.

Tightens the rules on corporate inversions: companies where former US owners keep 80% of the stock, and corporations managed and controlled from the United States, would be taxed as domestic companies.

Strengthens the base-erosion minimum tax (BEAT) by raising its rate to 12.5%, stopping companies from subtracting tax credits from the base, and lowering the threshold from $500 million to $25 million in gross receipts.

Denies foreign tax credits for payments to countries that give the company a specific economic benefit back — aimed at oil, gas, mining, and gambling companies making royalty-like 'tax' payments to foreign governments.

Limits tax treaty benefits for deductible payments between affiliates of foreign-controlled groups and repeals the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income (FDII), which today gives a reduced rate on profits attributed to foreign sales.

analysis.who_pays: US-headquartered multinational corporations and their shareholders would bear the cost through higher tax bills: a top rate of 35% instead of 21%, immediate taxation of foreign profits, loss of the FDII deduction, and new limits on interest deductions and treaty benefits. Companies that inverted their headquarters, and oil, gas, mining, and gambling companies using 'dual capacity' payments to foreign governments, face targeted tax increases. Some of the cost could ultimately reach consumers and workers through prices and wages, as economists generally expect corporate taxes to be shared among shareholders, workers, and customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: US multinational corporations and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The rate restoration applies to all corporations, not just multinationals: every corporation, including purely domestic ones, would pay graduated rates up to 35%, and personal service corporations would face a flat 35% — a large increase over the current 21% even for companies with no offshore activity.

Ending deferral would tax US shareholders on foreign subsidiary income currently and without regard to foreign taxes already paid, which risks double taxation and could put US multinationals at a disadvantage against foreign competitors that face no such rule.

Several provisions would apply 'without regard to any treaty obligation of the United States', overriding signed tax treaties — a step that could provoke disputes or retaliation from trading partners.

The interest-deduction limit would apply to any domestic corporation in an international group with average gross receipts over just $25 million, sweeping in mid-sized companies rather than only the largest multinationals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets genuine avoidance channels — deferral, check-the-box, inversions, profit stripping, haven-based cross-crediting — and its revenue would come from concentrated corporate interests. But it is a sweeping statement bill rather than a calibrated reform: restoring the 35% top rate for all corporations, taxing every dollar of foreign income currently, and unilaterally overriding tax treaties go well beyond what even many tax-policy experts on the anti-avoidance side propose, and the risks of double taxation, reduced investment, and treaty conflict are real. The worthwhile pieces (country-by-country credits, interest limits, inversion rules) were never separated out for consideration.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the Corporate Tax Dodging Prevention Act on April 10, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
Only two House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did.
The Ways and Means Committee never scheduled a markup or hearing, and the full House never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations and their shareholders came out ahead: the offshore deferral, check-the-box, FDII, and treaty-planning rules that the bill would have repealed all remained in place, and the corporate rate stayed at 21%.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: US multinationals that kept the current rules

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 10, 2024 and sponsored it.

for.name: 2 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other members joined.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Accepted the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Held the House majority and controlled the floor agenda
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote; the party majority declined to advance a large corporate tax increase.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes ever occurred, but every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat (3 of 216 House Democrats) and the Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee and House majority never acted on it.

industries.industry: US multinational corporations (tech, pharmaceuticals, and other overseas-heavy industries)
industries.note: The bill's heaviest lifters: their offshore profits would become immediately taxable, the FDII deduction would vanish, the top rate would rise to 35%, and interest stripping and treaty planning would be curtailed. Because the industry's savings under current law come from shifting profits away from where they are earned, its interest runs against ordinary taxpayers who would otherwise fund public services.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and mining companies with foreign operations
industries.note: The bill would deny foreign tax credits for 'dual capacity' payments — levies to foreign governments that come bundled with specific economic benefits to the company, common in extractive industries — raising their effective tax bills.

industries.industry: Companies that inverted their headquarters abroad
industries.note: Firms that moved their legal domicile overseas while keeping majority US ownership, and corporations managed from the United States, would be taxed as domestic companies again.
